questions.stem: The basic economic problem facing every society arises because
options: human wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited.
money is not always accepted as a medium of exchange.
some goods are produced in factories while others are produced on farms.
questions.explanation: Scarcity, unlimited wants set against limited resources, forces choice; it is the basic problem in every economy, rich or poor.

questions.stem: Funmilayo had ₦5,000 and could buy either a school bag or a pair of sandals. She bought the school bag. The pair of sandals she gave up is best described as the
options: opportunity cost of the school bag.
money cost of the school bag.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone; the sandals were the alternative sacrificed for the bag.

questions.stem: A list of a consumer's wants arranged in order of their importance is known as
questions.explanation: A scale of preference ranks wants from the most pressing to the least, helping the consumer choose with limited income.

questions.stem: A point lying inside a country's production possibility curve indicates that
options: the country is producing the maximum possible output.
the output combination cannot be attained with present resources.
some of the country's resources are unemployed or inefficiently used.
the country has experienced economic growth.
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPC show under-utilisation; points on it show full and efficient use; points outside are unattainable at present.

questions.stem: An outward shift of a country's production possibility curve can be caused by
options: a rise in the general price level.
the discovery of new mineral deposits.
a movement of workers from farming to manufacturing.
an increase in the rate of unemployment.
questions.explanation: New resources or better technology expand productive capacity and shift the whole PPC outwards; moving workers between sectors only moves the economy along the curve.

questions.stem: The production possibility curve is usually concave to the origin because
options: resources are equally suited to the production of all goods.
the opportunity cost of production is constant.
the opportunity cost of producing more of one good increases as more of it is produced.
consumers always prefer one good to another.
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally efficient in all uses, so each extra unit of one good requires giving up increasing amounts of the other.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a tertiary economic activity?
questions.explanation: Tertiary activities provide services such as banking, transport and insurance; fishing and lumbering are primary, manufacturing is secondary.

questions.stem: The conversion of crude oil into petrol and kerosene at a refinery in Port Harcourt is an example of
questions.explanation: Secondary production changes the form of raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods.

questions.stem: A country can produce either 600 bags of rice or 200 bicycles with its resources, and the opportunity cost is constant. What is the opportunity cost of producing one bicycle?
questions.explanation: With a constant trade-off, 200 bicycles cost 600 bags of rice, so one bicycle costs 600/200 = 3 bags.

questions.stem: The reward for land as a factor of production is
questions.explanation: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of land as a factor of production?
options: It bears the risks of production.
questions.explanation: Land is a free gift of nature whose total supply is fixed and which cannot be moved from place to place.

questions.stem: The factor of production that organises and coordinates the other factors and bears the uninsurable risks of business is
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur combines land, labour and capital and bears the non-insurable risks, earning profit as reward.

questions.stem: A tractor bought by a farmer in Kebbi State to plough his land is an example of
questions.explanation: Capital is man-made wealth used to produce further goods; the tractor is used for production, not for direct consumption.

questions.stem: Which of the following will most likely increase the efficiency of labour?
options: A reduction in the number of public holidays
An increase in the population of a country
A fall in the prices of consumer goods
questions.explanation: Training raises the skill and productivity of each worker; a larger population increases the quantity, not the efficiency, of labour.

questions.stem: Capital is said to depreciate because
options: its supply is fixed by nature.
it can only be used to produce one kind of good.
machines and equipment wear out with use and time.
the rate of interest falls over time.
questions.explanation: Capital goods lose value through wear and tear and obsolescence, so part of output must be set aside to replace them.

questions.stem: Occupational mobility of labour refers to the ease with which workers
options: move from one town to another.
move from one job to another.
questions.explanation: Occupational mobility is movement between jobs or occupations; geographical mobility is movement between places.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: In a capitalist economy, the major economic decisions are taken mainly through
questions.explanation: Under capitalism, private individuals respond to prices in free markets to decide what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: A major feature of a socialist economy is that
options: private profit is the main motive for production.
prices are determined only by demand and supply.
the means of production are owned and controlled by the state.
questions.explanation: In socialism the state owns most productive resources and central planners allocate them.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Nigeria is best described as a mixed economy because
options: it produces both agricultural and industrial goods.
it trades with both developed and developing countries.
both the government and private individuals own and control means of production.
it uses both cash and electronic money.
questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private enterprise with government ownership and regulation of some sectors.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: One disadvantage of a capitalist economy is that
options: it may lead to wide inequality in income and wealth.
questions.explanation: Free markets reward owners of resources unevenly, which can widen the gap between rich and poor.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: Which of the following questions is NOT one of the basic questions every economic system must answer?
options: For whom should goods be produced?
questions.explanation: The basic economic questions are what, how and for whom to produce (and how to provide for growth); who rules is a political question.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem: In a planned economy, the problem of "for whom to produce" is mainly solved by
options: the state deciding how goods are distributed among citizens.
consumers bidding for goods in the market.
firms producing for the highest bidders.
the forces of demand and supply.
questions.explanation: Under central planning, distribution is decided by government directives rather than by willingness to pay.

questions.stem: The arithmetic mean of the numbers 4, 8, 10, 6 and 12 is
The prices (in naira) of a loaf of bread in six shops are 900, 1,000, 850, 1,000, 950 and 1,100. What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often; ₦1,000 appears twice.

questions.stem: The daily sales (in units) of a kiosk over seven days were 12, 15, 9, 20, 15, 11 and 18. What is the median?
questions.explanation: Arranged in order: 9, 11, 12, 15, 15, 18, 20; the middle (4th) value is 15.

questions.stem: In a pie chart showing the expenditure of a family, food takes ₦36,000 out of a total monthly expenditure of ₦120,000. The angle of the sector for food is
Which of the following is most suitable for showing how a country's inflation rate changed month by month over two years?
questions.explanation: A line graph shows trends of a variable over time clearly; a pie chart shows shares of a whole at one point in time.

questions.stem: The ages of five workers are 22, 25, 30, 35 and x. If their mean age is 29 years, what is x?
Weekly wages (₦) of workers in a small workshop: 15,000 (3 workers), 20,000 (5 workers) and 30,000 (2 workers). The mean weekly wage is
The law of demand states that, other things being equal,
options: the higher the price of a commodity, the higher the quantity demanded.
quantity demanded is not affected by price.
the higher the price of a commodity, the lower the quantity demanded.
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded vary inversely, ceteris paribus, giving a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.stem: The demand for cement by building contractors is an example of
questions.explanation: Cement is wanted for the buildings it helps to produce, so its demand is derived from the demand for buildings.

questions.stem: Cars and petrol are said to be in
questions.explanation: Goods demanded together (complements) are in joint demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following will shift the demand curve for garri to the right?
options: An increase in the price of rice, a substitute
A fall in the price of garri
An increase in the price of garri
A fall in consumers' incomes, if garri is a normal good
questions.explanation: A rise in the price of a substitute raises demand for garri at every price; a change in garri's own price only causes movement along the curve.

questions.stem: A movement along a demand curve is caused by a change in
options: the price of the commodity itself.
questions.explanation: Only a change in own price moves along the curve; changes in other determinants shift the whole curve.

questions.stem: Palm oil is used for cooking, soap-making and the production of margarine. The demand for palm oil is therefore
questions.explanation: Composite demand arises when one commodity is demanded for several different uses.

questions.stem: When the price of a pen rises from ₦200 to ₦250, the quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80 units. The price elasticity of demand (using the original price and quantity) is
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = -20%; % change in price = +25%; elasticity = 20/25 = 0.8 (inelastic).

questions.stem: If the income elasticity of demand for a commodity is negative, the commodity is
questions.explanation: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises, giving a negative income elasticity.

questions.stem: The cross elasticity of demand between two goods is +1.5. The two goods are
questions.explanation: A positive cross elasticity means a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other, which is true of substitutes.

questions.stem: A trader finds that when she reduces the price of her bags, her total revenue falls. This means that the demand for her bags is
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, a price cut raises quantity proportionately less than the price fall, so total revenue falls.

questions.stem: The government wants to raise more revenue by imposing a tax on a commodity. It should choose a commodity whose demand is
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, quantity bought falls only slightly when the tax raises the price, so tax revenue is high.

questions.stem: Goods of ostentation, whose demand may rise as their price rises because they confer prestige, are examples of
questions.explanation: Prestige (Veblen) goods give an upward-sloping, exceptional demand curve.

questions.stem: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
options: more of a commodity is supplied at higher prices than at lower prices.
less of a commodity is supplied at higher prices.
supply is always equal to demand.
the price of a commodity is fixed by producers.
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable, so producers offer more; the supply curve slopes upwards.

questions.stem: Beef and hides are examples of goods in
questions.explanation: Producing one (beef) automatically produces the other (hides), so they are in joint (complementary) supply.

questions.stem: Which of the following will shift the supply curve of tomatoes to the left?
options: A fall in the price of fertilizer
A pest attack on tomato farms
A rise in the price of tomatoes
questions.explanation: A pest attack reduces the quantity offered at every price; the other changes increase supply or move along the curve.

questions.stem: A farmer can use his land to grow either maize or sorghum. Maize and sorghum are therefore in
questions.explanation: Resources used for one product cannot be used for the other at the same time, so the products are in competitive supply.

questions.stem: When the price of a commodity rises from ₦400 to ₦500, the quantity supplied rises from 200 to 300 units. The elasticity of supply is
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = 50%; % change in price = 25%; elasticity of supply = 50/25 = 2.0.

questions.stem: The supply of fresh fish brought to a market on a particular morning is likely to be
options: perfectly inelastic in the very short run.
highly elastic in the very short run.
questions.explanation: On the day, the quantity already brought cannot be changed whatever the price, so supply is fixed (perfectly inelastic).

questions.stem: Elasticity of supply tends to be greater
options: the longer the time period allowed for adjustment.
the more specialised the factors of production used.
the shorter the time period considered.
questions.explanation: Over a longer period producers can expand capacity and shift resources, so supply responds more to price changes.

questions.stem: A large increase in the demand for goat meat will most likely lead to
options: a decrease in the supply of goat skins.
a decrease in the price of goat meat.
an increase in the supply of goat skins.
no change in the supply of goat skins.
questions.explanation: Goat meat and skins are in joint supply; slaughtering more goats to meet the meat demand also raises the supply of skins.

questions.stem: Utility in economics refers to
options: the satisfaction derived from consuming a commodity.
the usefulness of a commodity to society as a whole.
the price paid for a commodity.
the cost of producing a commodity.
questions.explanation: Utility is the satisfaction or pleasure a consumer obtains from consuming a good or service.

questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as more units of a commodity are consumed,
options: the additional satisfaction from each successive unit eventually declines.
the price of the commodity falls.
questions.explanation: Each extra unit eventually adds less satisfaction than the one before, ceteris paribus.

questions.stem: Emeka's total utility from eating 1, 2 and 3 oranges is 20, 35 and 45 utils respectively. The marginal utility of the third orange is
questions.explanation: MU of the 3rd orange = TU(3) - TU(2) = 45 - 35 = 10 utils.

questions.stem: Use the total utility schedule: 1 unit = 30 utils, 2 units = 50 utils, 3 units = 60 utils, 4 units = 60 utils. Total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is
questions.explanation: MU of the 4th unit is 60 - 60 = 0; total utility stops rising (is maximised) when MU is zero.

questions.stem: A consumer spending her income on two goods X and Y is in equilibrium when
questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires the last naira spent on each good to give the same marginal utility.

questions.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying bread and milk. If the price of bread falls while everything else is unchanged, the consumer will
options: buy less bread because its utility has fallen.
buy the same quantities since her tastes have not changed.
spend all her income on milk.
buy more bread until MU/P is again equal for both goods.
questions.explanation: A lower price of bread raises MU/P for bread above that of milk, so she buys more bread until marginal utility falls and equality is restored.

questions.stem: The downward slope of the demand curve can be explained by
options: the law of diminishing marginal utility.
questions.explanation: As MU falls with each extra unit, the consumer will only buy more if the price is lower, giving a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.stem: Equilibrium price is the price at which
options: the government fixes the price of a commodity.
there is excess demand in the market.
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the market clears: buyers want exactly what sellers offer.

questions.stem: The demand and supply functions for a commodity are Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = 30 + P. The equilibrium price is
questions.explanation: Set 120 - 2P = 30 + P, so 90 = 3P and P = ₦30 (quantity = 60 units).

questions.stem: Given Qd = 120 - 2P and Qs = 30 + P, the equilibrium quantity is
If the demand for a commodity increases while supply remains unchanged, the equilibrium price will
options: rise and equilibrium quantity will rise.
fall and equilibrium quantity will rise.
rise and equilibrium quantity will fall.
questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand along an upward-sloping supply curve raises both price and quantity.

questions.stem: A good harvest of yam, with demand unchanged, is most likely to cause
options: a rise in the price of yam and a fall in quantity sold.
a rise in both price and quantity of yam.
no change in the price of yam.
a fall in the price of yam and a rise in the quantity sold.
questions.explanation: Supply shifts right, so the equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.

questions.stem: A maximum price fixed by government is likely to be effective only if it is set
questions.explanation: A ceiling has effect only when it holds price below the market-clearing level.

questions.stem: When a government fixes a maximum price for a commodity below the equilibrium price, the most likely result is
options: surplus of the commodity in the market.
shortage of the commodity and the emergence of a black market.
questions.explanation: At the lower price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied; the shortage encourages rationing and illegal sales above the control price.

questions.stem: A minimum wage fixed above the equilibrium wage rate is most likely to cause
options: unemployment, as the quantity of labour supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.
a fall in wages in the industry.
a rise in the quantity of labour demanded.
questions.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus; in the labour market the surplus is unemployment.

questions.stem: At a price of ₦50, quantity demanded is 400 units and quantity supplied is 250 units. This situation shows
options: excess supply of 150 units, which will push the price down.
excess demand of 150 units, which will push the price up.
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 400 - 250 = 150 units, so competition among buyers pushes price up.

questions.stem: Division of labour means
options: dividing the profits of a firm among its workers.
breaking production into separate processes, each done by different workers.
sharing a factory between two firms.
dismissing some workers to reduce costs.
questions.explanation: Division of labour splits a production task into stages, with workers specialising in particular stages.

questions.stem: One limitation of division of labour is
questions.explanation: Specialisation is profitable only if there is a large enough market to absorb the increased output.

questions.stem: A firm that enjoys a fall in average cost because it can buy raw materials in bulk at a discount is enjoying
questions.explanation: Bulk-buying discounts arise from the firm's own expansion, so they are internal (purchasing) economies.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an external economy of scale?
options: The provision of good roads and power to an industrial estate where many firms are located
A large firm's ability to employ specialised managers
A large firm's ability to borrow at lower interest
The use of large, efficient machines by a firm
questions.explanation: External economies come from the growth of the industry or area as a whole, not from the individual firm's size.

questions.stem: When 4 workers are employed, total product is 60 units; when a 5th worker is added, total product rises to 70 units. The marginal product of the 5th worker is
questions.explanation: MP = 70 - 60 = 10 units.

questions.stem: Using the data: 4 workers produce 60 units and 5 workers produce 70 units, the average product of labour when 5 workers are employed is
questions.explanation: AP = TP / L = 70 / 5 = 14 units.

questions.stem: The law of variable proportions states that as more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor,
questions.explanation: With at least one factor fixed, successive increments of the variable factor eventually add less and less to total product.

questions.stem: When marginal product is greater than average product, average product is
questions.explanation: If each additional unit adds more than the current average, the average must rise; MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.

questions.stem: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run are called
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as rent and insurance, must be paid whatever the level of output.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a variable cost for a bakery?
questions.explanation: Flour varies directly with the number of loaves baked; the others are fixed.

questions.stem: A firm's total fixed cost is ₦40,000 and its total variable cost for 200 units is ₦60,000. The average total cost is
Total cost of producing 10 units is ₦25,000 and that of 11 units is ₦26,800. The marginal cost of the 11th unit is
To the economist, the cost of a resource is best measured by
options: the money paid for it only.
its book value in the accounts.
the value of the best alternative forgone.
questions.explanation: The economist uses opportunity cost, which includes implicit costs that the accountant's money cost ignores.

questions.stem: In the short run, a firm should continue production even at a loss provided that its total revenue covers
questions.explanation: Fixed costs must be paid anyway; if revenue covers variable cost, producing reduces the loss compared with shutting down.

questions.stem: A trader sells 50 bags of rice at ₦75,000 each. Her total revenue is
A firm's total revenue is ₦9,000 when it sells 30 units and ₦9,500 when it sells 31 units. The marginal revenue of the 31st unit is
A market in which there is only one seller of a commodity with no close substitutes is
questions.explanation: A monopoly is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes and barriers to entry.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of perfect competition?
options: Entry into the industry is restricted.
questions.explanation: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge.

questions.stem: Under perfect competition, the demand curve facing an individual firm is
questions.explanation: The firm is a price taker and can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal.

questions.stem: Every firm, whatever the market structure, maximises profit where
options: total revenue is at its maximum.
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where MC = MR (with MC rising), since producing beyond this adds more to cost than to revenue.

questions.stem: Monopolistic competition is characterised by
options: one firm selling a unique product.
a few firms that are interdependent.
questions.explanation: Firms in monopolistic competition sell slightly different (branded) products, giving each some control over price.

questions.stem: In the long run, a firm under perfect competition earns
questions.explanation: Free entry attracts new firms when there are supernormal profits until price falls to minimum average cost, leaving only normal profit.

questions.stem: Price discrimination by a monopolist is possible only if
options: the product is sold in one market only.
buyers can easily resell the product between markets.
all buyers have the same elasticity of demand.
the markets can be kept separate and have different elasticities of demand.
questions.explanation: The seller must be able to prevent resale between markets, and the markets must respond differently to price.

questions.stem: A medical doctor who charges a lower fee to poor patients than to rich patients for the same treatment is practising
questions.explanation: Charging different prices to different buyers for the same service, for reasons not related to cost, is price discrimination.

questions.stem: A business owned and controlled by one person who bears all the risks is
questions.explanation: The sole proprietor provides the capital, takes all decisions and bears all risks and profits alone.

questions.stem: The liability of shareholders in a limited liability company is limited to
options: the amount of capital they have contributed or agreed to contribute.
the amount borrowed by the company.
questions.explanation: Shareholders can lose only the amount they invested or have agreed to pay for their shares.

questions.stem: A major source of finance available to a public limited company but not to a private limited company is
options: selling shares to the general public.
questions.explanation: Only a public company can invite the public to subscribe for its shares, for example through the stock exchange.

questions.stem: Which of the following is owned by government and provides essential services to the public?
questions.explanation: Public corporations are set up by an Act or law, owned by government and run mainly to provide services rather than to maximise profit.

questions.stem: The sale of government-owned shares in public enterprises to private individuals and firms is called
questions.explanation: Privatisation transfers ownership from the state to private investors.

questions.stem: Commercialisation of a public enterprise means that
options: the enterprise is sold to private investors.
the enterprise is taken over by foreigners.
the enterprise remains government-owned but is run on a profit-making basis.
questions.explanation: In commercialisation, ownership stays with government, but the enterprise is expected to cover its costs and make profit without subsidies.

questions.stem: A policy by which a government takes over the ownership and control of privately owned enterprises is
questions.explanation: Nationalisation transfers private enterprises to state ownership.

questions.stem: The chain of distribution for most manufactured consumer goods is
questions.explanation: Goods typically pass from the producer to wholesalers, who sell in smaller lots to retailers, who sell to final consumers.

questions.stem: One function of the wholesaler to the manufacturer is
options: selling goods in small units to final consumers.
buying in bulk and relieving the manufacturer of storage problems.
fixing the retail price of goods.
questions.explanation: Bulk purchase by wholesalers gives manufacturers ready cash and frees them from storing large stocks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a problem of distribution in many West African countries?
questions.explanation: Bad transport infrastructure raises costs and delays in moving goods from producers to consumers.

questions.stem: Middlemen are often blamed for high prices because
options: they produce goods at high cost.
they reduce the supply of money.
they pay low taxes to government.
each middleman adds a profit margin as goods pass along the chain.
questions.explanation: Every intermediary adds its own margin, so long chains of distribution can raise final prices.

questions.stem: A manufacturer may choose to sell directly to consumers, bypassing wholesalers, especially when
options: the product is standardised and sold in small quantities across the country.
the product is perishable or made to order.
the manufacturer lacks capital for retail outlets.
questions.explanation: Perishable or custom-made goods need quick delivery and direct contact with buyers, so direct selling is preferred.

questions.stem: The movement of people from villages to towns in search of jobs is called
questions.explanation: Rural-urban migration is the internal movement of people from rural areas to cities, usually in search of jobs and amenities.

questions.stem: A population census is
options: an official count of all the people in a country at a particular time.
a record of births in a hospital.
a survey of the labour force only.
the registration of voters for elections.
questions.explanation: A census counts the whole population and collects data on age, sex, occupation and location.

questions.stem: According to Thomas Malthus, population tends to grow
options: in arithmetic progression while food supply grows in geometric progression.
at the same rate as food supply.
in geometric progression while food supply grows in arithmetic progression.
questions.explanation: Malthus argued that population outruns food supply, leading to positive checks such as famine and disease.

questions.stem: A country has a population of 80 million. If its birth rate is 38 per thousand and its death rate is 13 per thousand, what is its natural increase in one year (ignoring migration)?
questions.explanation: Natural growth rate = 38 - 13 = 25 per thousand = 2.5%; 2.5% of 80 million = 2 million.

questions.stem: Optimum population is the size of population at which
options: the birth rate equals the death rate.
the country has the largest population in its region.
output per head is at its maximum, given the available resources.
every person is employed in agriculture.
questions.explanation: At the optimum, resources are combined with the population in a way that gives the highest income per head.

questions.stem: A high dependency ratio in a developing country is mainly caused by
options: a large proportion of people aged 15 to 64 years.
a large proportion of children below working age.
questions.explanation: High birth rates give a youthful population, so many dependants rely on a relatively small working-age group.

questions.stem: One problem of conducting a population census in many West African countries is
options: inadequate funding and logistics for enumerators to reach all areas.
the absence of any population to count.
excess accurate birth and death records.
questions.explanation: Poor funding, difficult terrain, illiteracy and political interference make accurate counts difficult.

questions.stem: The labour force of a country consists of
options: people of working age who are willing and able to work, whether employed or not.
all the people in the country.
questions.explanation: The labour force includes the employed and the unemployed who are actively seeking work.

questions.stem: Unemployment that results when workers lose their jobs because machines have replaced them is called
questions.explanation: Technological (structural) unemployment arises when new technology reduces the need for certain skills.

questions.stem: Farm labourers who have no work during the dry season experience
questions.explanation: Work in agriculture depends on seasons, so workers may be idle for part of the year.

questions.stem: Underemployment exists when
options: workers are employed below their skills or work fewer hours than they wish.
there are more vacancies than job seekers.
questions.explanation: Underemployed workers have jobs but are not using their full capacity, skills or desired hours.

questions.stem: A trade union can raise the wages of its members without causing unemployment if
options: the demand for their labour is elastic.
the supply of labour is increasing rapidly.
the demand for their labour is inelastic.
questions.explanation: When labour demand is inelastic, a higher wage reduces the number employed only slightly.

questions.stem: The supply of labour to an industry will increase if
options: the wage rate in the industry rises relative to other industries.
the industry's working conditions become more dangerous.
training periods for the job become longer.
questions.explanation: Higher relative wages attract workers from other industries, increasing the quantity of labour supplied.

questions.stem: Human capital refers to
options: money saved by workers in banks.
the knowledge, skills and health that make workers more productive.
the total population of a country.
questions.explanation: Investment in education, training and health builds human capital, raising labour productivity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an export crop in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Cocoa is grown mainly for export, while yam, cassava and millet are mainly food crops for local consumption.

questions.stem: Subsistence (peasant) farming is characterised by
options: production mainly for the farmer's family consumption.
questions.explanation: Peasant farmers use simple tools, small plots and family labour, producing mainly for their own needs.

questions.stem: The supply of agricultural products tends to fluctuate widely mainly because
options: output depends on weather and other natural conditions.
farmers are always paid fixed prices.
the demand for food is perfectly elastic.
questions.explanation: Rainfall, pests and diseases cause large unplanned changes in harvests.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a major problem of agriculture in West Africa?
options: Poor storage and processing facilities leading to post-harvest losses
questions.explanation: A lot of produce is lost after harvest because of poor storage, processing and transport.

questions.stem: The main purpose of a guaranteed minimum price for an agricultural product is to
options: increase the prices paid by consumers.
protect farmers' incomes from a sharp fall in prices.
questions.explanation: A guaranteed minimum price stabilises farmers' incomes and encourages continued production.

questions.stem: A bumper harvest may reduce farmers' total income because
options: the demand for most food crops is price inelastic.
the demand for food crops is price elastic.
the supply of food is perfectly inelastic.
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, the large fall in price needed to sell the extra output reduces total revenue.

questions.stem: Agriculture contributes to industrial development by
options: reducing the supply of food to towns.
increasing the cost of labour in industry.
providing raw materials for agro-based industries.
questions.explanation: Crops such as cotton, cocoa and oil palm feed textile, food-processing and other agro-allied industries.

questions.stem: An industrial estate is
options: a large farm owned by government.
the head office of a company.
an area of land set aside and provided with facilities for factories.
questions.explanation: Industrial estates provide roads, power, water and other facilities to attract firms to one area.

questions.stem: The concentration of a particular industry in a particular area is known as
questions.explanation: Localisation means firms of the same industry cluster in one place, gaining external economies.

questions.stem: A cement factory is usually located near the source of limestone mainly because
options: the raw material is bulky and loses weight in processing.
questions.explanation: Weight-losing raw materials are expensive to transport, so firms locate near them.

questions.stem: Import substitution industrialisation is a strategy in which a country
options: produces locally goods that were formerly imported.
questions.explanation: The aim is to save foreign exchange and build local industries by producing goods previously imported.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a major problem of industrialisation in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Unreliable power raises production costs as firms rely on expensive generators.

questions.stem: The distinction between a plant and a firm is that a plant is
options: a group of firms producing similar goods.
a business that sells only agricultural products.
a single unit of production such as a factory, while a firm owns and controls one or more plants.
questions.explanation: A firm is the business unit that owns and controls production; a plant is a single factory or workplace.

questions.stem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of
options: all goods produced by citizens abroad.
all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
questions.explanation: GDP measures the market value of final output produced within the country's borders, usually in a year.

questions.stem: Gross National Product (GNP) is equal to GDP
options: plus net factor income from abroad.
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + (factor income received from abroad - factor income paid abroad).

questions.stem: Given GNP = ₦80 trillion and depreciation (capital consumption) = ₦6 trillion, the Net National Product is
questions.explanation: NNP = GNP - depreciation = 80 - 6 = ₦74 trillion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included when measuring national income by the income approach?
options: Pensions paid to retired civil servants
questions.explanation: Pensions are transfer payments, not payments for current production, so they are excluded to avoid overstating income.

questions.stem: Double counting in national income accounting occurs when
options: the value of intermediate goods is counted together with that of final goods.
questions.explanation: Counting intermediate goods (e.g. flour) and the final good (bread) together overstates output.

questions.stem: Using the expenditure approach: consumption = ₦50bn, investment = ₦20bn, government spending = ₦15bn, exports = ₦12bn and imports = ₦9bn. GDP is
A country's national income rose from ₦500bn to ₦600bn, while its population rose from 50 million to 60 million. Per capita income
questions.explanation: 500bn/50m = ₦10,000 and 600bn/60m = ₦10,000, so income per head is unchanged.

questions.stem: One limitation of national income figures as a measure of living standards is that they
options: include the value of all final goods.
do not take account of how income is distributed among the population.
questions.explanation: A high average income may hide wide inequality; non-market output and quality of life are also left out.

questions.stem: Exchange of goods for goods without the use of money is called
questions.explanation: Barter is direct exchange of goods and services without money.

questions.stem: The main problem of barter is
options: the need for a double coincidence of wants.
questions.explanation: Each trader must find someone who has what he wants and wants what he has.

questions.stem: When money is used to compare the values of different goods, it is performing its function as
options: a unit of account (measure of value).
questions.explanation: As a unit of account, money provides a common measure in which the values of goods are expressed.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics of good money ensures that it can be divided into smaller units for small transactions?
questions.explanation: Divisibility allows money to be split into smaller denominations without loss of value.

questions.stem: Keynes' transactions motive for holding money refers to holding money
options: to take advantage of changes in bond prices.
to lend to others at interest.
questions.explanation: The transactions motive is for regular purchases between paydays; the precautionary motive is for emergencies; the speculative motive concerns bond prices.

questions.stem: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), if V and T are constant and the money supply doubles, the price level will
questions.explanation: With velocity and transactions fixed, P varies in direct proportion to M.

questions.stem: The value of money is said to fall when
questions.explanation: When prices rise, each naira buys fewer goods, so its purchasing power (value) falls.

questions.stem: Inflation is best defined as
options: a once-and-for-all rise in the price of one commodity.
a persistent rise in the general price level.
a fall in the general price level.
an increase in the number of banks.
questions.explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices over time.

questions.stem: Inflation caused by rising costs of production such as wages and fuel prices is called
questions.explanation: When firms pass on higher input costs to buyers, the result is cost-push inflation.

questions.stem: Which group of people is most likely to lose during inflation?
options: Holders of real assets such as land
questions.explanation: Fixed incomes buy less as prices rise; debtors gain because they repay with money of lower value.

questions.stem: The Consumer Price Index rose from 200 in one year to 230 in the next. The rate of inflation is
Which of the following measures is most suitable for controlling demand-pull inflation?
options: Raising the monetary policy rate to discourage borrowing
Reducing the cash reserve ratio of banks
questions.explanation: A higher policy rate makes credit dearer, reducing aggregate demand; the other measures increase spending.

questions.stem: A very rapid and uncontrollable rise in prices, in which money almost loses its value, is called
questions.explanation: Hyperinflation involves extremely high rates of price increase that destroy confidence in money.

questions.stem: Demand-pull inflation occurs when
options: the price of imported raw materials rises.
firms raise prices to increase profit margins.
aggregate demand exceeds the available supply of goods and services.
questions.explanation: "Too much money chasing too few goods" describes demand-pull inflation.

questions.stem: The bank that issues currency and acts as banker to the government in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The CBN issues the naira, is banker to government and to commercial banks, and conducts monetary policy.

questions.stem: The Central Bank acts as "lender of last resort" by
options: lending to members of the public directly.
lending to commercial banks when they face temporary liquidity problems.
questions.explanation: It provides emergency funds to banks to prevent bank failures and loss of public confidence.

questions.stem: The capital market deals in
options: short-term funds such as treasury bills only.
long-term funds such as shares and bonds.
questions.explanation: The capital market provides long-term finance; the money market deals in short-term funds.

questions.stem: A commercial bank creates credit mainly because
options: it holds all deposits as cash.
it needs to keep only a fraction of its deposits as cash reserves.
it is owned by the government.
questions.explanation: Since depositors do not withdraw all their money at once, banks lend out most deposits, creating new deposits.

questions.stem: If the cash reserve ratio is 20% and a commercial bank system receives a fresh deposit of ₦100,000, the maximum total deposits that can be created in the banking system is
questions.explanation: Credit multiplier = 1 / 0.2 = 5; total deposits = 5 x 100,000 = ₦500,000.

questions.stem: Treasury bills are
options: long-term loans given by banks to farmers.
short-term government securities sold at a discount.
bills paid by government to contractors.
questions.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term (usually up to one year) debt instruments of government traded on the money market.

questions.stem: Which of the following specialises in giving long-term loans for building or buying houses?
questions.explanation: Mortgage banks and building societies provide long-term housing finance secured on property.

questions.stem: A tax imposed on goods and services, such as value added tax, is
questions.explanation: Indirect taxes are levied on spending and can be shifted to consumers; direct taxes are on income and wealth.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct tax?
questions.explanation: Personal income tax is paid directly by the person on whom it is levied.

questions.stem: A tax system in which the rate of tax increases as income increases is
questions.explanation: Under progressive taxation, higher incomes pay a higher percentage in tax.

questions.stem: Kemi earns ₦100,000 and pays ₦10,000 tax; Bayo earns ₦300,000 and pays ₦30,000. This tax is
questions.explanation: Both pay 10% of their income, so the rate is constant: a proportional tax.

questions.stem: Adam Smith's canon of taxation which states that the time and manner of payment should be convenient to the taxpayer is the canon of
questions.explanation: The canon of convenience requires taxes to be collected when and how it is easiest for the taxpayer.

questions.stem: Government expenditure on the construction of new roads and bridges is classified as
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure creates durable assets; recurrent expenditure covers salaries, maintenance and other running costs.

questions.stem: When a tax is imposed on a commodity whose demand is perfectly inelastic, the incidence of the tax falls
questions.explanation: Consumers buy the same quantity whatever the price, so the producer can pass the whole tax on in a higher price.

questions.stem: A budget deficit occurs when
options: planned government expenditure exceeds expected revenue.
questions.explanation: A deficit budget is financed by borrowing or drawing on reserves and is often used to stimulate the economy.

questions.stem: The national debt of a country refers to
options: the total outstanding amount the government owes to domestic and foreign lenders.
the amount citizens owe to banks.
the value of imports for a year.
the total taxes collected in a year.
questions.explanation: The national (public) debt is the accumulated borrowing of government, both internal and external.

questions.stem: Economic development differs from economic growth in that development
options: refers only to an increase in GDP.
includes improvements in welfare, such as health, education and reduced poverty.
questions.explanation: Growth is a rise in real output; development also involves structural change and better living standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of developing countries?
options: Heavy dependence on primary products for export earnings
questions.explanation: Developing economies often rely on a few primary exports, have low incomes and rapid population growth.

questions.stem: A development plan that is reviewed and extended by one year at the end of each year is called
questions.explanation: A rolling plan is continually updated, adding a new year as each year is completed.

questions.stem: A long-term plan covering a period of 15 to 30 years is known as
questions.explanation: Perspective plans set broad long-term goals, which are implemented through shorter plans.

questions.stem: A major problem of development planning in many West African countries is
questions.explanation: Plans based on poor data give unrealistic targets; other problems include poor implementation, corruption and policy instability.

questions.stem: The vicious circle of poverty describes a situation in which
options: high income leads to high savings and high investment.
low income leads to low savings, low investment, low productivity and again low income.
questions.explanation: Low incomes limit saving and investment, keeping productivity and incomes low.

questions.stem: International trade arises mainly because
options: all countries produce the same goods.
there is no money in some countries.
countries are endowed with different resources and skills.
questions.explanation: Differences in natural resources, climate, skills and technology make countries better at producing different goods.

questions.stem: Country A can produce 10 tonnes of cocoa or 5 tonnes of rice per worker; country B can produce 6 tonnes of cocoa or 4 tonnes of rice per worker. According to comparative advantage,
options: A should specialise in cocoa and B in rice.
A should specialise in rice and B in cocoa.
A should produce both goods and B neither.
there is no basis for trade.
questions.explanation: In A, 1 rice costs 2 cocoa; in B, 1 rice costs 1.5 cocoa. B has the lower opportunity cost in rice, A in cocoa.

questions.stem: The terms of trade of a country are calculated as
options: (index of export prices / index of import prices) x 100.
(value of exports / value of imports) x 100.
(index of import prices / index of export prices) x 100.
questions.explanation: Terms of trade compare export prices with import prices.

questions.stem: In a year, a country's export price index was 120 and its import price index was 150. Its terms of trade were
questions.explanation: Terms of trade = 120 / 150 x 100 = 80, which is unfavourable (below 100).

questions.stem: A tariff calculated as a percentage of the value of an imported good is
questions.explanation: Ad valorem duties are percentages of value; specific duties are fixed amounts per unit.

questions.stem: A complete ban on the importation of a particular commodity is
questions.explanation: An embargo prohibits trade in the item entirely; a quota merely limits the quantity.

questions.stem: The major export of Nigeria by value is
questions.explanation: Crude oil and gas account for the large majority of Nigeria's export earnings.

questions.stem: The balance of trade is the difference between
options: total receipts and total payments of a country.
the value of visible exports and visible imports.
the value of invisible exports and invisible imports.
questions.explanation: Balance of trade covers only visible (merchandise) trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an invisible export for Nigeria?
options: Fees paid by foreign tourists visiting Obudu Mountain Resort
questions.explanation: Services such as tourism, shipping and insurance earned from foreigners are invisible exports.

questions.stem: A country's visible exports are ₦900bn and visible imports ₦1,100bn; invisible exports are ₦400bn and invisible imports ₦150bn. The current account shows
questions.explanation: Visible balance = -200; invisible balance = +250; current account = +50, a surplus.

questions.stem: Devaluation of a country's currency is intended to
options: make exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.
increase the external value of the currency.
questions.explanation: Devaluation lowers the external value of the currency, encouraging exports and discouraging imports.

questions.stem: Devaluation will improve a country's balance of payments only if
options: the demand for its exports is perfectly inelastic.
the demand for its exports and imports is sufficiently elastic.
its imports are mainly essential goods with inelastic demand.
other countries also devalue their currencies.
questions.explanation: If demand is inelastic, export earnings may not rise enough and import spending may not fall enough to improve the balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a measure for correcting a balance of payments deficit?
options: Restricting imports through tariffs and quotas
Increasing the external value of the currency
questions.explanation: Import restrictions reduce payments abroad; the other options worsen the deficit.

questions.stem: A floating exchange rate system is one in which
options: the central bank fixes the rate permanently.
the currency is tied to the value of gold.
foreign exchange is rationed by government.
the exchange rate is determined by the demand for and supply of the currency.
questions.explanation: Under a floating system, market forces of demand and supply set the rate.

questions.stem: ECOWAS was established in 1975 by the Treaty of
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was founded on 28 May 1975 by the Treaty of Lagos; its Commission is headquartered in Abuja.

questions.stem: A form of economic integration in which member countries remove trade barriers among themselves but each keeps its own tariffs against non-members is
questions.explanation: A customs union adds a common external tariff; a common market adds free movement of factors.

questions.stem: A customs union differs from a free trade area in that member countries
options: adopt a common external tariff against non-members.
questions.explanation: The common external tariff is the distinguishing feature of a customs union.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a problem facing ECOWAS?
options: Identical currencies in all member states
Poor transport links among member countries
questions.explanation: Poor roads and railways, differing currencies and the withdrawal of some members limit integration.

questions.stem: Which of the following countries withdrew from ECOWAS with effect from January 2025?
questions.explanation: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left ECOWAS in January 2025, having formed the Alliance of Sahel States.

questions.stem: The headquarters of the African Development Bank is in
questions.explanation: The AfDB, founded in 1964, has its headquarters in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire.

questions.stem: The main function of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to
options: fix the prices of crude oil.
provide short-term assistance to member countries with balance of payments problems.
regulate trade among African countries only.
questions.explanation: The IMF promotes exchange rate stability and lends to members facing balance of payments difficulties.

questions.stem: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) is also known as
questions.explanation: The IBRD, set up at Bretton Woods in 1944, is the main lending arm of the World Bank Group.

questions.stem: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) mainly aims to
options: build refineries in all member countries.
coordinate the petroleum policies of member countries to stabilise oil prices.
questions.explanation: OPEC coordinates production policies to secure fair and stable prices for petroleum producers.

questions.stem: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) is particularly important to developing countries because it
options: sets quotas for crude oil production.
issues a common currency for them.
seeks fairer terms of trade and better market access for their exports.
questions.explanation: UNCTAD works to integrate developing countries into the world economy on fair terms.

questions.stem: Nigeria's crude oil is produced mainly in
questions.explanation: Most of Nigeria's oil and gas is found in the Niger Delta, onshore and offshore.

questions.stem: A negative effect of crude oil production on the Nigerian economy has been
options: neglect of agriculture as the economy became dependent on oil.
the creation of a large export earnings base.
questions.explanation: Heavy reliance on oil led to neglect of agriculture and vulnerability to oil price swings (the "Dutch disease").

questions.stem: Gold has been a major export of
questions.explanation: Ghana (formerly the Gold Coast) is one of Africa's leading gold producers.

questions.stem: Oil spillage in the Niger Delta has affected the local economy mainly by
options: destroying farmland and fishing waters, reducing local incomes.
questions.explanation: Pollution damages land and water, harming farming and fishing livelihoods.

questions.stem:
The table below shows the demand schedule for sachets of groundnut oil in a market in Kano.
Price (₦): 500, 600, 700, 800, 900
Quantity demanded (sachets per week): 1,200, 1,000, 800, 600, 400
(a) Calculate the total revenue (total expenditure) at each price. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate the price elasticity of demand when price rises from ₦600 to ₦700, using the original price and quantity. [4 marks]
(c) Is demand elastic or inelastic over this range? Give a reason. [3 marks]
(d) At what price is total revenue highest? [2 marks]
(e) State three factors, other than price, that determine the demand for groundnut oil. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) TR = 600,000; 600,000; 560,000; 480,000; 360,000 (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) % change in Qd = -200/1,000 x 100 = -20% (1); % change in P = 100/600 x 100 = 16.67% (1); PED = 20/16.67 (1) = 1.2 (1)
3 marks: (c) Elastic (1) because the coefficient 1.2 is greater than 1 / the price rise reduced total revenue from ₦600,000 to ₦560,000 (2)
2 marks: (d) Total revenue is highest (₦600,000) at both ₦500 and ₦600 (2)
6 marks: (e) Any three, 2 marks each: income of consumers; prices of substitutes (e.g. palm oil); prices of complements; tastes and preferences; size of population; expectation of future price changes; seasons/festivals; advertising
questions.explanation: (a) TR = P x Q: ₦500 x 1,200 = ₦600,000; ₦600 x 1,000 = ₦600,000; ₦700 x 800 = ₦560,000; ₦800 x 600 = ₦480,000; ₦900 x 400 = ₦360,000. (b) Quantity falls by 200 from 1,000 (20%) while price rises by ₦100 from ₦600 (16.67%); PED = 20 / 16.67 = 1.2. (c) Demand is elastic because the coefficient exceeds one; consistent with this, total revenue fell when price rose. (d) Total revenue is highest, ₦600,000, at ₦500 and at ₦600. (e) Other determinants include consumers' income, prices of substitutes such as palm oil, prices of complements, tastes, population size, price expectations, festive seasons and advertising.

questions.stem:
The table shows the cost of a small sachet-water factory in Ibadan. Fixed cost is ₦20,000 at every level of output.
Output (bags): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Total cost (₦): 20,000, 30,000, 36,000, 45,000, 58,000, 75,000
(a) Calculate the total variable cost at each output level. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the average total cost at outputs of 10, 30 and 50 bags. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the marginal cost for each additional 10 bags. [5 marks]
(d) If each bag sells for ₦1,500, calculate the profit or loss at output 40 and output 50. [4 marks]
(e) Distinguish between fixed cost and variable cost, giving one example of each from the factory. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) TVC = 0; 10,000; 16,000; 25,000; 38,000; 55,000 (half mark each)
3 marks: (b) ATC = 3,000 at 10; 1,500 at 30; 1,500 at 50 (1 mark each)
5 marks: (c) MC per 10 bags = 10,000; 6,000; 9,000; 13,000; 17,000 (1 mark each), i.e. ₦1,000, ₦600, ₦900, ₦1,300 and ₦1,700 per bag
4 marks: (d) At 40 bags: TR = 60,000, profit = ₦2,000 (2); at 50 bags: TR = 75,000, profit = ₦0, break-even (2)
5 marks: (e) Fixed cost does not vary with output in the short run (1), e.g. rent of the factory/salary of manager (1); variable cost changes directly with output (1), e.g. nylon sachets/water treatment chemicals/fuel (1); fixed costs are incurred even at zero output (1)
questions.explanation: (a) TVC = TC - TFC: 0, 10,000, 16,000, 25,000, 38,000 and 55,000. (b) ATC = TC/Q: 30,000/10 = ₦3,000; 45,000/30 = ₦1,500; 75,000/50 = ₦1,500. (c) MC for each block of 10 bags: 10,000; 6,000; 9,000; 13,000; 17,000 (i.e. ₦1,000, ₦600, ₦900, ₦1,300, ₦1,700 per bag). (d) At 40 bags TR = ₦60,000 and TC = ₦58,000, a profit of ₦2,000; at 50 bags TR = ₦75,000 = TC, so the firm breaks even. (e) Fixed costs such as rent and the manager's salary do not change with output and are paid even when nothing is produced; variable costs such as sachets, chemicals and diesel rise and fall with output.

questions.stem:
The data below relate to the economy of a West African country for one year (₦ billion).
Private consumption expenditure: 4,500
Gross private investment: 1,200
Government purchases of goods and services: 1,300
Exports of goods and services: 1,600
Imports of goods and services: 1,400
Net factor income from abroad: -300
Capital consumption (depreciation): 450
Indirect taxes: 500
Subsidies: 100
(a) Calculate: (i) Gross Domestic Product at market prices; (ii) Gross National Product at market prices; (iii) Net National Product at market prices; (iv) National Income (NNP at factor cost). [12 marks]
(b) Explain why net factor income from abroad is negative for many developing countries. [4 marks]
(c) State two uses of national income statistics. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) GDP = C + I + G + (X - M) = 4,500 + 1,200 + 1,300 + 200 = ₦7,200bn
3 marks: (a)(ii) GNP = GDP + NFIA = 7,200 - 300 = ₦6,900bn
3 marks: (a)(iii) NNP = GNP - depreciation = 6,900 - 450 = ₦6,450bn
3 marks: (a)(iv) NI = NNP - indirect taxes + subsidies = 6,450 - 500 + 100 = ₦6,050bn
4 marks: (b) Foreign firms operating in the country repatriate profits and dividends; interest is paid on foreign debt; payments to expatriate workers exceed income earned by citizens abroad (any two, 2 marks each)
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: to measure economic growth; to compare living standards over time/between countries; for economic planning; to show the structure/contribution of sectors; to guide government policy and budgeting
questions.explanation: (a) GDP = 4,500 + 1,200 + 1,300 + (1,600 - 1,400) = ₦7,200bn. GNP = 7,200 + (-300) = ₦6,900bn. NNP = 6,900 - 450 = ₦6,450bn. National income at factor cost = 6,450 - 500 + 100 = ₦6,050bn. (b) Net factor income is negative because foreign-owned firms send profits home, the country pays interest on external loans and pays expatriates, while its own citizens earn relatively little from investments and work abroad. (c) National income data are used to measure growth, compare standards of living, plan development, show sectoral structure and guide fiscal policy.

questions.stem:
The following are extracts from the balance of payments of a country (in $ million).
Merchandise exports: 9,500
Merchandise imports: 11,200
Services received from abroad: 1,800
Services paid abroad: 2,600
Net income (investment income): -900
Net current transfers (e.g. remittances from citizens abroad): 3,100
(a) Calculate: (i) the balance of trade; (ii) the balance on services; (iii) the current account balance. [9 marks]
(b) State whether the current account is in surplus or deficit. [2 marks]
(c) Explain three measures the country can use to correct a persistent balance of payments deficit. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Balance of trade = 9,500 - 11,200 = -$1,700m (deficit)
3 marks: (a)(ii) Balance on services = 1,800 - 2,600 = -$800m
3 marks: (a)(iii) Current account = -1,700 - 800 - 900 + 3,100 = -$300m
2 marks: (b) The current account is in deficit of $300m
9 marks: (c) Any three, explained, 3 marks each: devaluation/depreciation of the currency to make exports cheaper and imports dearer; import restrictions (tariffs, quotas, embargo); export promotion (incentives, subsidies, diversification); exchange control; contractionary monetary and fiscal policies to reduce demand for imports; borrowing from the IMF/use of external reserves to finance the gap; encouraging foreign direct investment
questions.explanation: (a) Trade balance = 9,500 - 11,200 = -$1,700m; services = 1,800 - 2,600 = -$800m; current account = -1,700 - 800 - 900 + 3,100 = -$300m. (b) The current account is in deficit by $300m; remittances reduce but do not eliminate the deficit. (c) Remedies include devaluation, tariffs and quotas, export promotion and diversification, exchange control, deflationary monetary/fiscal policy, attracting foreign investment and financing the gap from reserves or IMF loans.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following concepts: (i) scarcity; (ii) choice; (iii) opportunity cost. [9 marks]
(b) With the aid of a production possibility curve described in words, explain how a country's decision to produce more military equipment affects its production of food. [7 marks]
(c) Give two reasons why the production possibility curve of a country may shift outwards. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) Scarcity: resources are limited relative to human wants, which are unlimited
3 marks: (a)(ii) Choice: because of scarcity, individuals/governments must decide which wants to satisfy and which to leave unsatisfied, using a scale of preference
3 marks: (a)(iii) Opportunity cost: the alternative forgone when a choice is made / the next best alternative sacrificed
2 marks: (b) A PPC shows the maximum combinations of two goods (military equipment and food) that can be produced with fully employed resources
3 marks: (b) Producing more military equipment means moving along the curve, withdrawing resources from food production
2 marks: (b) The food forgone is the opportunity cost of the extra military equipment, and it increases as more equipment is produced (concave curve)
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: discovery of new resources; improvement in technology; increase in the quantity/quality of labour (education, training); increase in capital stock through investment
questions.explanation: (a) Scarcity means resources (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship) are limited compared with unlimited wants. Choice is the decision on which wants to satisfy, guided by a scale of preference. Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone. (b) A PPC plots the maximum output combinations of two goods. Moving resources to military equipment moves the economy along the curve towards more equipment and less food; the food given up is the opportunity cost, which rises as more resources less suited to arms are switched. (c) The curve shifts outwards with new resources, better technology, a larger or better-trained workforce and more capital goods.

questions.topic: Types and Basic Features of Economic Systems
questions.stem:
(a) What is a mixed economy? [3 marks]
(b) State four features of a mixed economy. [8 marks]
(c) Explain three reasons why governments in West Africa participate directly in economic activities. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) An economic system in which both the private sector and the government own and control the means of production, and decisions are made by both the price mechanism and government
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: co-existence of private and public sectors; private ownership of property alongside state enterprises; price mechanism operates with government regulation; profit motive and welfare motive both exist; government provides essential/social services; government controls strategic industries; consumer sovereignty is partly limited by government regulation
9 marks: (c) Any three, explained, 3 marks each: to provide essential services that private firms may not provide (e.g. water, electricity, roads); to prevent exploitation by private monopolies; to provide services requiring huge capital; to reduce income inequality; to create employment; for national security in strategic industries; to promote balanced development of regions; to raise revenue
questions.explanation: (a) A mixed economy combines private enterprise and market prices with public ownership and government regulation, as in Nigeria and Ghana. (b) Features include co-existence of public and private sectors, private property, government regulation of prices and standards, both profit and welfare motives, and state control of strategic sectors. (c) Governments participate to provide public utilities and infrastructure that need huge capital or yield low profit, to control monopolies, to create jobs, to redistribute income, to protect strategic and security interests and to promote balanced regional development.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between maximum price legislation and minimum price legislation. [6 marks]
(b) Explain, with the aid of a diagram described in words, the effects of fixing a maximum price for petrol below the equilibrium price. [8 marks]
(c) State three measures government may adopt to make the maximum price effective. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Maximum price: a legal price ceiling above which a commodity must not be sold, fixed below equilibrium to protect consumers
3 marks: (a) Minimum price: a legal floor below which price must not fall, fixed above equilibrium to protect producers/workers (e.g. minimum wage, guaranteed farm prices)
2 marks: (b) Diagram: demand and supply curves crossing at equilibrium price; a horizontal line below equilibrium shows the maximum price
2 marks: (b) At the maximum price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage
2 marks: (b) Queues and hoarding develop, and black markets arise where petrol sells above the control price
2 marks: (b) Suppliers may reduce supply or divert products across borders (smuggling)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: rationing (e.g. coupons or quotas per buyer); government subsidy to suppliers; direct government supply/importation to increase supply; strict enforcement and penalties against hoarding and black-marketeering; price control inspectors/monitoring
questions.explanation: (a) A maximum price is a ceiling below equilibrium meant to protect consumers; a minimum price is a floor above equilibrium meant to protect producers or workers. (b) With the ceiling below equilibrium, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls, creating excess demand; long queues, hoarding, black markets and smuggling follow. (c) Government may ration supply, subsidise producers, increase supply directly and enforce the control with penalties and inspectors.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a monopoly? [3 marks]
(b) State four sources of monopoly power. [8 marks]
(c) Explain three differences between a monopolist and a firm under perfect competition. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) A market structure in which there is a single seller of a commodity that has no close substitutes, with barriers preventing entry
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: legal backing/statutory monopoly; patents and copyrights; control of essential raw materials; economies of scale (natural monopoly); huge capital requirement as a barrier; mergers/amalgamations; tariff protection; exclusive franchise
9 marks: (c) Any three, 3 marks each: one seller versus many sellers; monopolist is a price maker while the competitive firm is a price taker; downward-sloping demand (AR) curve versus a horizontal demand curve; barriers to entry versus free entry and exit; monopolist can earn supernormal profit in the long run versus only normal profit; monopolist can practise price discrimination; product has no close substitutes versus homogeneous products
questions.explanation: (a) A monopoly is the sole producer/seller of a product without close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry. (b) Monopoly power comes from law (statutory monopolies), patents, control of raw materials, economies of scale, large capital requirements, mergers and tariff protection. (c) The monopolist is a single price-making seller facing a downward-sloping demand curve, protected by entry barriers and able to keep supernormal profit and discriminate in price; a perfectly competitive firm is one of many price-takers facing a horizontal demand curve and earns only normal profit in the long run.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a public corporation? [3 marks]
(b) State four reasons why government establishes public corporations. [8 marks]
(c) Explain three problems that have led to the privatisation of public corporations in Nigeria. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) A business enterprise set up by an Act/law of parliament or a decree, owned and financed by government and run to provide essential services
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: to provide essential services/public utilities; to prevent private monopoly exploitation; to undertake projects needing huge capital; to control strategic industries; to create employment; to generate revenue; to promote balanced regional development
9 marks: (c) Any three, explained, 3 marks each: inefficiency and poor service delivery; mismanagement and corruption; political interference in appointments and operations; over-staffing; huge losses and dependence on government subsidies; lack of accountability; outdated equipment due to poor maintenance
questions.explanation: (a) A public corporation is a statutory body owned by government and run, often at low or no profit, to provide services such as water, power or ports. (b) Government creates them to supply essential services, control strategic sectors, avoid private monopoly, fund capital-intensive projects, create jobs and raise revenue. (c) Many were privatised because of inefficiency, corruption, political interference, over-staffing, chronic losses and heavy subsidies, and poor maintenance.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the Malthusian theory of population. [8 marks]
(b) State three criticisms of the theory. [6 marks]
(c) State three problems of rapid population growth in a developing country. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Population tends to grow in geometric progression (1, 2, 4, 8, ...)
2 marks: (a) Food supply grows in arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, 4, ...) because of diminishing returns on land
2 marks: (a) Population will outstrip food supply, leading to misery and poverty
2 marks: (a) Population is checked by positive checks (famine, war, disease) or preventive checks (late marriage, moral restraint)
6 marks: (b) Any three, 2 marks each: Malthus underestimated technological progress in agriculture; he did not foresee birth control; food production has grown faster than population in many countries; international trade allows importation of food; population growth can also increase the labour force and output; his rates of growth were not supported by evidence
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: pressure on social amenities (schools, hospitals, housing); high unemployment; high dependency ratio; low savings and investment; food shortages; environmental degradation and urban congestion
questions.explanation: (a) Malthus (1798) argued that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population outruns food unless checked by famine, disease and war or by preventive checks such as late marriage. (b) Critics note that technology raised farm output, birth control spread, trade allows food imports and population growth may add to output. (c) Rapid growth strains amenities, raises unemployment and dependency, reduces savings and investment, and causes food shortages, congestion and environmental damage.

questions.stem:
(a) Define unemployment. [2 marks]
(b) Explain four types of unemployment. [12 marks]
(c) State three ways government can reduce unemployment among school leavers in Nigeria. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A situation in which people who are willing and able to work at the existing wage rate cannot find jobs
12 marks: (b) Any four, explained, 3 marks each: frictional (between jobs/lack of information); seasonal (due to seasons, e.g. farming); structural (decline of an industry/change in demand pattern); cyclical/demand-deficient (during depression/recession); technological (replacement of workers by machines); disguised (more workers than needed, zero marginal product); residual (physically/mentally challenged)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: skills acquisition and vocational training programmes; credit support for small businesses/youth entrepreneurship schemes; revitalising industries through stable power and infrastructure; expanding agriculture through incentives; review of school curriculum to emphasise skills; labour-intensive public works
questions.explanation: (a) Unemployment exists when people able and willing to work at current wages cannot find jobs. (b) Types include frictional, seasonal, structural, cyclical, technological and disguised unemployment, each with its distinct cause. (c) Government can promote vocational skills, give credit for small businesses, fix power and infrastructure to revive industry, support agriculture, reform curricula and run labour-intensive public works.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four reasons why agriculture is important to the economy of a West African country. [12 marks]
(b) Explain four measures that can be taken to improve agricultural production. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) Any four, 3 marks each: provides food for the population; provides raw materials for industries; source of employment for a large part of the labour force; earns foreign exchange through exports; source of government revenue; provides market for industrial goods; contributes to GDP; releases labour and capital for industry
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: provision of credit facilities to farmers; supply of improved seedlings and subsidised fertilizers; mechanisation; extension services and training; improved storage and processing facilities; rural infrastructure (roads, irrigation); guaranteed minimum prices; land reforms; pest and disease control
questions.explanation: (a) Agriculture feeds the population, supplies raw materials to industry, employs many people, earns foreign exchange, provides revenue and markets for industrial goods and contributes significantly to GDP. (b) Output can be raised through credit, improved inputs, mechanisation, extension services, better storage and processing, rural roads and irrigation, guaranteed prices, land reform and pest control.

questions.stem:
(a) What is money? [3 marks]
(b) Explain four functions of money. [12 marks]
(c) State two problems associated with the barter system. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Anything generally acceptable as a means of payment for goods and services and in settlement of debts
12 marks: (b) Any four, 3 marks each: medium of exchange; unit of account/measure of value; store of value; standard of deferred payment
5 marks: (c) Any two (award 3 and 2): double coincidence of wants; lack of a common measure of value; indivisibility of some goods; difficulty of storing wealth; difficulty of deferred payment; high transport cost of goods
questions.explanation: (a) Money is anything generally accepted as payment for goods and services and settlement of debts, such as the naira. (b) Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, a store of value and a standard of deferred payment. (c) Barter suffers from the double coincidence of wants, absence of a common measure, indivisibility, storage problems and difficulty of deferred payments.

questions.stem:
(a) What is inflation? [3 marks]
(b) Explain three causes of inflation. [9 marks]
(c) Explain four ways in which the Central Bank can use monetary policy to control inflation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) A persistent rise in the general price level over a period of time, which reduces the value of money
9 marks: (b) Any three, 3 marks each: excess demand over supply (demand-pull); rising costs of production such as wages, fuel and imported inputs (cost-push); increase in money supply/excessive government deficit spending; depreciation of the currency (imported inflation); shortage of goods due to poor harvest or insecurity; hoarding and speculation
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: raising the monetary policy rate; open market operations (selling securities); raising the cash reserve ratio; raising the liquidity ratio; selective credit controls; moral suasion; special deposits
questions.explanation: (a) Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money.
