(b) Causes include demand-pull pressure, cost-push factors such as higher fuel and wage costs, excessive money supply and deficit financing, currency depreciation, supply shortages and hoarding. (c) The Central Bank can raise the policy rate, sell securities in open market operations, raise reserve and liquidity ratios, use selective credit controls, moral suasion and special deposits to reduce credit and spending.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five functions of a commercial bank. [10 marks]
(b) Explain five functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Any five, 2 marks each: accepting deposits; granting loans and overdrafts; facilitating payments (cheques, electronic transfers); safe keeping of valuables; acting as agent/executor for customers; foreign exchange services; financial advice; credit creation; discounting bills of exchange
10 marks: (b) Any five, 2 marks each: issuing currency; banker to government; banker to commercial banks; lender of last resort; controlling money supply/monetary policy; managing foreign reserves; supervising and regulating banks; managing the public debt; promoting financial stability and payment systems
questions.explanation: (a) Commercial banks accept deposits, lend through loans and overdrafts, provide payment services, keep valuables, act as agents and executors, deal in foreign exchange, advise customers and create credit. (b) The CBN issues the naira, banks for government and commercial banks, acts as lender of last resort, controls money and credit, manages external reserves and public debt and regulates the banking system.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain four canons of taxation. [12 marks]
(b) Distinguish between direct and indirect taxes, giving two examples of each. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) Any four, 3 marks each: equality/equity (tax according to ability to pay); certainty (amount, time and manner known); convenience (time and manner convenient to taxpayer); economy (cost of collection low relative to yield); flexibility; simplicity; productivity
4 marks: (b) Direct tax is levied on income/wealth and borne by the person on whom it is imposed (burden cannot be shifted) (2); indirect tax is levied on goods and services and can be shifted to consumers (2)
4 marks: (b) Examples: direct, e.g. personal income tax, company income tax, capital gains tax (2); indirect, e.g. value added tax, import duty, excise duty (2)
questions.explanation: (a) The canons are equality (ability to pay), certainty, convenience and economy, with later additions such as flexibility, simplicity and productivity. (b) Direct taxes fall on income and wealth and are borne by the taxpayer (personal income tax, company income tax); indirect taxes fall on goods and services and can be passed on (VAT, import and excise duties).

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between economic growth and economic development. [6 marks]
(b) Explain four characteristics of developing countries. [8 marks]
(c) State three problems of development planning in West Africa. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Economic growth is a sustained increase in a country's real output/GDP over time
3 marks: (a) Economic development is growth accompanied by structural change and improvement in living standards (health, education, reduced poverty and inequality)
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: low per capita income; dependence on primary production; high population growth rate; low level of technology; high unemployment and underemployment; poor infrastructure; low savings and capital formation; dualistic economy; high illiteracy
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: inadequate data; shortage of funds; political instability and policy reversals; corruption; lack of skilled manpower; poor implementation and monitoring; over-dependence on foreign aid
questions.explanation: (a) Growth is a quantitative increase in real GDP; development is qualitative and includes structural transformation and improved welfare. (b) Developing countries typically have low incomes, dependence on primary products, rapid population growth, low technology, unemployment, poor infrastructure and low savings. (c) Planning is hindered by poor data, lack of funds, policy instability, corruption, skill shortages, weak implementation and dependence on aid.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the principle of comparative cost advantage. [6 marks]
(b) Using the following data, show which country should specialise in which product. With equal resources, Nigeria can produce 40 units of yam or 20 units of cloth; Ghana can produce 30 units of yam or 10 units of cloth. [8 marks]
(c) State three limitations of the theory of comparative cost advantage. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) A country should specialise in producing the goods in which it has the lowest opportunity cost (greatest comparative advantage), even if it has an absolute advantage in both, and trade for others; total output rises
2 marks: (b) Nigeria: 1 cloth costs 2 yam; 1 yam costs 0.5 cloth
2 marks: (b) Ghana: 1 cloth costs 3 yam; 1 yam costs 1/3 cloth
4 marks: (b) Nigeria has a comparative advantage in cloth (lower opportunity cost, 2 < 3 yam) and should specialise in cloth (2); Ghana has a comparative advantage in yam (1/3 < 1/2 cloth) and should specialise in yam (2)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: assumes no transport costs; assumes free trade with no barriers; assumes perfect mobility of factors within countries; assumes constant costs; ignores dangers of over-specialisation; considers only two countries and two goods; ignores exchange rates
questions.explanation: (a) Comparative advantage holds that a country gains by specialising in goods with the lower opportunity cost and exchanging them. (b) Nigeria has an absolute advantage in both goods, but its opportunity cost of cloth (2 yam) is lower than Ghana's (3 yam), while Ghana's opportunity cost of yam (1/3 cloth) is lower than Nigeria's (1/2 cloth). Nigeria should specialise in cloth and Ghana in yam. (c) The theory ignores transport costs, trade barriers, factor immobility, increasing costs, the dangers of over-specialisation and the many-country, many-goods reality.

questions.stem:
(a) What is economic integration? [3 marks]
(b) State four objectives of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). [8 marks]
(c) Explain three problems that hinder the effective operation of ECOWAS. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) The coming together of countries, usually in a region, to remove trade barriers among themselves and coordinate economic policies for mutual benefit
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: promote trade among member states by removing tariffs and non-tariff barriers; free movement of persons, goods and services; establish a common external tariff; harmonise economic and monetary policies; promote joint development of infrastructure (transport, energy, telecommunications); promote regional peace and security; raise living standards of the people of the region
9 marks: (c) Any three, 3 marks each: political instability and coups leading to suspension or withdrawal of members (e.g. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left in 2025); multiplicity of currencies; poor transport and communication links; similar primary products limiting intra-regional trade; non-implementation of protocols/border harassment; loyalty to former colonial powers/language differences; inadequate funding by members; smuggling
questions.explanation: (a) Economic integration is the merging of economies of a group of countries through removal of trade barriers and harmonisation of policies. (b) ECOWAS aims to promote intra-regional trade, free movement of people and goods, a common external tariff, harmonised policies, joint infrastructure and regional peace. (c) ECOWAS is hampered by political instability and withdrawals, many currencies, poor transport links, similar exports, failure to implement protocols, colonial and language ties and poor funding.

questions.stem:
(a) State four contributions of the petroleum industry to the Nigerian economy. [8 marks]
(b) Explain four negative effects of the petroleum industry on the Nigerian economy. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) Any four, 2 marks each: major source of foreign exchange; major source of government revenue; provides employment; provides raw materials for petrochemical industries; provides energy/fuel for industry and transport; attracts foreign investment; development of infrastructure in oil areas
12 marks: (b) Any four, 3 marks each: neglect of agriculture and other sectors (mono-economy); environmental pollution from oil spills and gas flaring; vulnerability to fall in world oil prices; restiveness and insecurity in oil-producing areas; rural-urban migration; corruption and rent-seeking; loss of farmland and fishing waters
questions.explanation: (a) Petroleum provides most of Nigeria's foreign exchange and a large share of government revenue, employment, energy and raw materials, and attracts foreign investment. (b) It has led to neglect of agriculture, pollution and gas flaring, exposure to oil price shocks, unrest in producing areas, migration and corruption.
